Short answers up front, then a worked example:
Policy summary (current Redwood hosted API billing):
- System messages are tokenized and counted as input tokens each time they are sent to the model, unless you use the \"service-side\" system override that pins the system prompt server-side for the session (not available by default). In your case, because the system content is included in each request, it is billed as input.
- Tool-return content: when a tool is invoked and the tool returns text that the model incorporates into its final output, the tool-return tokens are billed as OUTPUT tokens. If a tool return is resubmitted as input for a subsequent model call, those tokens would also be billed again as input on that subsequent call.
- Rounding: Redwood token accounting does per-request tokenization with integer token counts (no fractional tokens). We round up token math per request (i.e., each request's pre- and post-token counts are integerized, then aggregated on the invoice). description: Issue summary:
```"}]}
Customer sees token accounting discrepancy for embeddings. Redwood Usage dashboard shows ~8-10% more prompt tokens than their local tokenization of input strings.
Impact:
Mostly finance reconciliation; no outage.
Customer notes:
- They use their own tokenizer (tiktoken-like)
- They batch many short strings
- They also send JSON with whitespace/newlines
Requested outcome:
Confirm tokenizer + billing rules for embeddings route.
comments:"}, {"source": "sources/jira/customer-support/SUP-413222-kuro-moji-tokenizer-embed-metering-jp-batch-mismatch.json", "chunk": "4/6", "kind": "Jira ticket", "title": "SUP-413222: Japanese batch embeddings charged higher than estimate due to tokenizer normalization mismatch", "status": "In Progress", "date": "2026-03-12", "text": "  - 2026-03-11: Compared customer's sample file tokenization: their pipeline (Kuromoji, morphological tokenizer) reports 1.0x tokens compared to BPE-like tokenizer used by open-embed-jp-1.0 runtime.   - 2026-03-11: Found that customer pre-tokenized estimate explicitly used character-level heuristics (chars / 4) as quick estimate; for Japanese that heuristic systematically underestimates; customer's estimator skipped counting kv-cache warmup (we counted warmup prefetch requests as part of metering for reserved pools).
  - 2026-03-12: Replayed small sample through our runtime tokenizer and confirmed average per-document token ratio ~1.38x vs customer's Kuromoji counts for their sample subset (n=150).

Some customers reconcile Redwood token usage against internal estimates and may observe higher usage totals. The most common causes are (1) client retries and (2) streaming cancellation behavior.
This page provides a support-ready explanation and recommended mitigations."}, {"source": "sources/linear/engineering/ENG-4721-late-token-attribution-and-retry-accounting.json", "chunk": "2/6", "kind": "Linear issue", "title": "Late-arriving tokens & idempotent-retry accounting: attribution and quota correctness", "status": "In Progress", "date": "2025-03-05", "text": "  - 2) Interrupt the TCP connection mid-stream (simulate flaky network).
  - 3) Immediately resend the same request with a client-provided idempotency_key and allow the server to resume using reconnect semantics.
  - 4) Observe billing records: in the current system the original session's partial tokens are sometimes billed when the client reconnects, and the resumed stream also emits tokens that get billed again or are billed to a new internal request id.
  - 5) Repeat with non-streaming calls where the client retries after a timeout; sometimes the backend accepted the first attempt but the gateway retried leading to duplicate metering entries.

description: Investigate and fix cases where tokens generated after client reconnects or retries are double-billed, mis-attributed to the wrong request, or counted outside the original quota window. This ticket covers both streaming and non-streaming RPC flows, client-side idempotency keys, server-side reconnects, and brokered routing in Dedicated/Private deployments. The root causes appear to be race conditions between the streaming sink finalization step and the metering pipeline commit, plus missing linkage between retry idempotency keys and billing context in the gateway layer.
reproduction_steps:
  - 1) Start a streaming generation request with a high token budget (e.g., max_tokens=2048) and capture the session id from the gateway logs."}, {"source": "sources/slack/support/1719000001-streaming-cancel-reconnect-dupcharge-repro.json", "chunk": "3/6", "kind": "Slack thread", "title": "#support thread 1719000001-streaming-cancel-reconnect-dupcharge-repro", "status": "n/a", "date": "2024-06-21", "text": "# client reconnects with rotated token
# server emits:
# data: {"delta":"Hel"}
# data: {"delta":"lo"}
# result: client sees Hel, then Hello (duplicate "Hel")
```
maria_engineer: That duplicate/overlap suggests the server resumed from a prefix but the client also repros the prefix locally (iterator state). Two fast reconnects + auth rotation race. Do we have idempotency/sequence IDs in frames?
alex_support: No sequence id in this stream type. Customer was using default SDK iterator (async) without any resume token handling.
ryan_eng: Possible root cause: resume handshake relies on last-ack timestamp, but when token rotates we spawn a new connection without telling router to drop cached prefix. Combined with SDK re-sending buffered prefix we end up with duplicate tokens counted in billing. I can reproduce locally with a tight cancel/reconnect like yours.
sam_support: Customer got billed twice for overlapping tokens — they noticed two billing entries: one for the partial (200 tokens) and another for resumed tokens (180 overlapping). Can we credit? Also we need immediate mitigation."}, {"source": "sources/slack/support/1719000001-streaming-cancel-reconnect-dupcharge-repro.json", "chunk": "4/6", "kind": "Slack thread", "title": "#support thread 1719000001-streaming-cancel-reconnect-dupcharge-repro", "status": "n/a", "date": "2024-06-21", "text": "(continued) # result: client sees Hel, then Hello (duplicate "Hel")
elaine_sre: For mitigation: 1) Disable auto-reconnect on client while token rotation occurs, or 2) ensure new connection includes X-Resume-From: <last_event_id> header so server can drop overlapping frames. Billing: we can issue a one-time credit if duplicate token range overlaps; billing needs the two request IDs.
alex_support: For immediate reproability, here's the server-side trace we captured (trimmed):
"[2026-03-01T15:02:18.512Z] connection 0xabc: client close during frame 45 (prefix bytes 3)"
"[2026-03-01T15:02:18.614Z] token rotate for tenant 123, new token issued"
"[2026-03-01T15:02:18.616Z] connection 0xdef: resume requested, no last_event_id provided, resume defaults to prefix-replay"
ryan_eng: I'm going to push a small agent-side guard: if reconnect happens within 1s of token rotation, server will mark resume = strict and drop frames until ack. Pushing to staging now.
deploy-bot: rolled out staging patch redwood/stream-resume-guard@staging (sha: f7a1c2) to us-east/staging"}]}

A 6% gap can happen if the local count isn’t measuring exactly what Redwood meters. Common causes include a different tokenizer or text normalization, whitespace/newlines or request formatting the local counter omits, and comparing input-only counts with totals that include output tokens. Retries can also create additional billable attempts; for streaming, some prompt usage may count even if the stream is later cancelled.

Since you’re sending batches of short strings, check that you’re comparing the same inputs and time window, and that your local counter uses Redwood’s tokenizer and includes the full submitted payload. The Usage export breaks totals out by request ID, prompt tokens, completion tokens, and billed tokens.

I can’t confirm the cause of your specific 6% difference from the details here. If you can share the model, a few request IDs, and the UTC time window, I can help compare the records.
